mcqs.q: Dental caries is defined as:
opts: An infectious microbial disease of the calcified tissues, with demineralization and organic destruction
mcqs.explain: Caries is an infectious microbial disease of calcified tooth tissues — demineralization of the inorganic part and destruction of the organic part.

mcqs.q: Caries is classified by:
mcqs.explain: Caries is classified by location (where), extent (how deep) and rate (how fast).

mcqs.q: Primary caries is best described as:
opts: The original (first) carious lesion of the tooth
mcqs.explain: Primary caries is the original/first carious lesion; secondary (recurrent) caries occurs at the margin of an existing restoration.

mcqs.q: Pit-and-fissure caries arises from:
opts: Imperfect coalescence of developmental enamel lobes
mcqs.explain: Pit-and-fissure caries forms in pits/fissures from imperfect coalescence of enamel lobes; on reaching the DEJ it spreads laterally.

mcqs.q: Smooth-surface caries begins:
opts: On a smooth enamel area habitually covered by plaque
mcqs.explain: Smooth-surface caries starts on a smooth enamel area that is habitually unclean and covered by plaque (not in a pit/fissure).

mcqs.q: Root-surface caries progresses faster than enamel caries because:
opts: The thin cementum provides little resistance to caries attack
mcqs.explain: The cementum covering the root is extremely thin and offers little resistance, so root caries is faster; it is common in older patients with gingival recession.

mcqs.q: Secondary (recurrent) caries occurs:
opts: At the junction of a restoration and the tooth
mcqs.explain: Secondary/recurrent caries occurs at the restoration-tooth junction and may progress under the restoration, usually indicating microleakage.

mcqs.q: Secondary caries usually indicates the presence of:
mcqs.explain: Recurrent caries at a restoration margin signals microleakage and other caries-conducive conditions.

mcqs.q: Incipient caries is:
opts: The first, reversible enamel change (a white spot) that can be remineralized
mcqs.explain: Incipient caries is the first evidence of activity — an opaque white spot when air-dried — and is reversible/remineralizable with fluoride and plaque control.

mcqs.q: Remineralization of an incipient lesion is promoted by:
mcqs.explain: Early/incipient lesions can be remineralized by fluoride application and plaque removal before cavitation occurs.

mcqs.q: Cavitated caries:
opts: Has a broken enamel surface, usually into dentin, and needs preparation/restoration
mcqs.explain: In cavitated (non-reversible) caries the enamel is broken and the lesion has reached dentin; remineralization is no longer possible, so restoration is needed.

mcqs.q: Acute (rampant) caries is characterised by:
opts: Rapidly progressing, soft, light-coloured lesions affecting many teeth
mcqs.explain: Acute (rampant) caries progresses rapidly, with soft, light-coloured lesions in many teeth.

mcqs.q: Chronic (arrested) caries typically appears:
opts: Hard and brown-to-black, and may be more caries-resistant
mcqs.explain: Arrested/chronic caries is slow or stopped, hard and brown-to-black (a fluoride effect), sometimes more resistant than adjacent enamel.

mcqs.q: 'Forward caries' refers to caries that:
opts: Extends from the pit/fissure toward the DEJ and then into dentin
mcqs.explain: Forward caries proceeds from enamel to the DEJ to dentin; backward caries spreads laterally at the DEJ and back into enamel.

mcqs.q: A tooth preparation involving TWO surfaces is termed:
mcqs.explain: By surfaces: simple = one surface, compound = two surfaces, complex = three or more surfaces.

mcqs.q: In G.V. Black's classification, Class I lesions are:
mcqs.explain: Class I = pit-and-fissure lesions (occlusal of posteriors, buccal/lingual pits, lingual pits of anteriors).

mcqs.q: Class II cavities are located on the:
mcqs.explain: Class II involves the proximal surfaces of posterior teeth (premolars and molars).

mcqs.q: A Class III cavity is on the:
opts: Proximal surface of an anterior tooth NOT involving the incisal angle
mcqs.explain: Class III = proximal of anterior teeth without involving the incisal angle; Class IV includes the incisal angle.

mcqs.q: A Class IV cavity differs from a Class III in that it:
opts: Involves the incisal angle of the anterior tooth
mcqs.explain: Class IV is a proximal lesion of an anterior tooth that involves the incisal angle.

mcqs.q: Class V cavities are located in the:
opts: Cervical (gingival) third of facial or lingual surfaces
mcqs.explain: Class V lesions occur in the cervical/gingival third of the facial or lingual surfaces of any tooth.

mcqs.q: Class VI (Simon's addition) cavities involve the:
mcqs.explain: Class VI involves the incisal edges of anterior teeth and the cusp tips of posterior teeth.

mcqs.q: 'Residual caries' is caries that:
opts: Remains in a completed preparation, by intention or accident
mcqs.explain: Residual caries remains in a completed preparation; it is unacceptable on prepared enamel walls but affected dentin may be left near the pulp.

saqs.a: An infectious microbial disease of the calcified tooth tissues, with demineralization of the inorganic and destruction of the organic portion.

saqs.q: Give the three morphologic types of primary caries by location.
Why is root caries faster, and who is affected?
saqs.a: The thin cementum gives little resistance, so it progresses faster; common in older patients with gingival recession.
Incipient: reversible white spot, remineralizable with fluoride. Cavitated: broken enamel into dentin, non-reversible, needs restoration.
Acute (rampant): rapid, soft, light-coloured, many teeth. Chronic (arrested): slow/stopped, hard, brown-black.

saqs.q: Classify tooth preparations by number of surfaces.
Match G.V. Black Classes I–V to their locations.
saqs.a: I pits/fissures; II proximal posterior; III proximal anterior (no incisal angle); IV proximal anterior + incisal angle; V cervical third.
